text: Picture the moment a second team asks for cloud access. Someone creates a fresh subscription or account, hands over the login, and the team starts building. At that instant, nothing about it is governed — no logging, no network connectivity to anything else the company runs, no policy stopping a public storage bucket. That's the default state of every new subscription or account on both Azure and AWS. This lesson is about why that gap gets expensive, and what actually closes it.

In that blank state, there's no identity baseline — just a local admin login instead of the company's real identity provider. There's no network path to shared services, so the team is on its own for connectivity and DNS. And there's no active policy, so nothing technically prevents a misconfigured, publicly exposed resource or an untagged one nobody can trace to a budget. Building first and adding governance later fails here, because retrofitting any of that onto resources that already exist is a project in itself.

A landing zone is a pre-provisioned, pre-governed environment a new workload lands into, with all of that already solved. Identity is wired to the real identity provider. Network connectivity to shared services is already peered in. Policy guardrails are actively enforced, not documented on a wiki page. Logging and cost tracking are centralized from the first resource created. None of this is one product — it's a pattern, built on Azure from management groups and policy, and on AWS from Organizations and Control Tower.

The reason timing matters is simple: the cost of adding governance scales with how much already exists without it. Retrofitting a tagging standard onto two hundred existing resources is expensive. Retrofitting network segmentation after a dev environment has quietly been talking to production for months is an incident, not a project. Building identity, networking, and policy in before the first resource exists costs almost nothing by comparison, which is the economic argument for the whole pattern.

A single team on one account can skip most of this with little visible cost — there's no one else to isolate from yet. The pattern pays for itself the moment a second team shows up, inheriting an already-built baseline in minutes instead of a manual setup project with its own gaps. Next lesson picks up Azure's specific implementation: management groups, platform versus landing zone subscriptions, and subscription vending as a repeatable process.
